prompt: The nginx finding JTB-2026-02 on `web` cannot be fixed by its due date: the fixed package breaks the portal's proxy settings. ana, in IT, writes an exception with a rate limit at the edge as the compensating control, and plans to approve it herself, with no expiry, because she knows the server best. What turns it into a legitimate risk decision?
hint: Information Security Fundamentals, lesson 3; Endpoint Defence and Hardening, lesson 16.

choices.text: The asset's risk owner signs it, and it lapses on a set date
choices.why: IT proposes the controls and the owner of the asset accepts what is left. An exception without an expiry is how a finding becomes permanent.

choices.text: Nothing more: the rate limit mitigates the risk, so nothing is left to accept
choices.why: Every treatment except avoidance leaves a residual risk, and somebody with the authority has to accept it.

choices.text: Recording it as transferred to the vendor, whose ticket is still open
choices.why: A ticket moves no consequences anywhere. Even a real transfer leaves the accountability with the business that chose the supplier.

choices.text: Calling it avoidance, since port 80 now limits how fast anybody can reach nginx
choices.why: Avoidance means stopping the activity that creates the risk. The portal still runs the vulnerable nginx.

prompt: The SOC reviews the sign-in detector of the shop's week. At threshold 3, with `svc-backup` left out, `detect.py` printed TP 9, FP 5, FN 2 and TN 75. What is that detector's false positive rate, in percent?
hint: Information Security Fundamentals, lesson 11.

prompt: A rule on the portal's log fires at 03:10 on one account. The first line is `192.168.10.20 ana "GET /payslips/bruno HTTP/1.1" 403 -`, and within a few minutes the same account asks for carla, diego and twenty more names, every answer 403. What does the analyst read in this, and what comes next?
hint: Information Security Fundamentals, lesson 8; SOC, Monitoring and Incident Response, lesson 7.

choices.text: Somebody is guessing ana's password and the 403s are sign-ins the portal refused, so the address gets blocked
choices.why: A failed sign-in is 401, and these lines carry ana's name because the requests authenticated.

choices.text: The portal has just told the caller which names are on the payroll, so the payroll is now exposed
choices.why: The portal refuses on permission before it checks existence, so every name gets the same 403 and nothing is learnt.

choices.text: ana's account proved who it is and wants what it is not allowed; ask her, and escalate if it was not her
choices.why: A rise in 403s is an authenticated identity exploring or a wrong role. Whether it is expected is a question for ana or her manager, recorded in the note.

choices.text: Nothing happened, since every request was refused, so the alert closes as a false positive with that reason
choices.why: The rule matched exactly what it describes. Closing a true alert without asking is the costliest mistake in triage.

prompt: On Thursday at 02:33, after 57 failures over 19 accounts, `203.0.113.66` logged in to `gw` as bruno with a password. Which of these would be a second factor in lesson 9's sense, so that the guessed password alone would no longer have been enough? Choose all that apply.
hint: Information Security Fundamentals, lesson 9; SOC, Monitoring and Incident Response, lesson 7.

choices.text: A six-digit TOTP code from the authenticator app on bruno's phone
choices.why: Something he has. Whoever guessed the password does not hold the secret the codes are computed from.

choices.text: The answer to a security question bruno chose when he joined
choices.why: Something he knows, like the password, and lost the same ways. The login is longer and no stronger in kind.

choices.text: A rule that refuses logins from countries the firm does no business in
choices.why: Location is a signal that raises or lowers suspicion, not evidence of who somebody is.

choices.text: A push approval on bruno's phone, with number matching
choices.why: Possession of the phone, and number matching stops the tap-yes-to-make-it-stop defeat.

choices.text: A second password, which bruno must keep different from the first
choices.why: Two passwords are one factor: both are something you know.

choices.text: A security key that signs a challenge for the address it was registered with
choices.why: Possession of a key that never leaves the device, and the strongest of the four in the lesson.

prompt: A review of the portal finds staff passwords stored as Argon2id hashes and the TOTP secrets stored encrypted, under a key from the secrets manager. A colleague asks for the TOTP secrets to be hashed with Argon2id as well, "like the passwords". Why would that break MFA?
hint: Information Security Fundamentals, lesson 9; Applied Cryptography, lesson 5.

choices.text: Argon2id would mix a salt per account into each secret, so the codes the server computes would stop matching the phone's
choices.why: The phone never sees the stored value. The trouble is that the server could no longer get the secret back at all.

choices.text: To check a code the server computes it from the secret, so it needs the secret back, and a hash gives nothing back
choices.why: A password only has to be recognised, so a one-way hash is enough. A TOTP check is an HMAC computed with the secret itself.

choices.text: Nothing would break, but it adds nothing either, since TOTP secrets are random already
choices.why: It would break every login: once only a hash is stored, nothing can compute the expected code.

choices.text: Argon2id is too slow to run inside one 30-second step
choices.why: Its cost is what one password sign-in already pays. The problem is that a hash cannot be turned back into the key.

prompt: The clinic calls its AWS access Zero Trust: staff sign in through the identity provider with MFA, and dani was disabled there the week her contract ended in March. In October the credential report still has her row as `dani,false,true,...`: no MFA, an active access key, used today. What does this row mean for that claim?
hint: Information Security Fundamentals, lesson 7; Cloud Security, lesson 6.

choices.text: Nothing, because AWS still checks every request against the key's policy, which is the enforcement point
choices.why: That check asks what the key may do. It never asks who holds the key or from what device, which is the decision lesson 7 puts in front of every resource.

choices.text: The key should have been limited to the office network, which would have kept it safe
choices.why: Location grants nothing under Zero Trust. A key accepted from the office is still a key anybody inside can hold.

choices.text: It is the break-glass identity that every design keeps outside the provider, so it is expected there
choices.why: A break-glass user has a hardware key in a safe and is never used. This one is used, has no MFA and belongs to somebody who left.

choices.text: Identity is the perimeter, and this identity sits outside the provider that decides, with no MFA
choices.why: When location stops deciding, identity does. An IAM user the leavers process never touches is an unlocked door beside the one that is guarded.

prompt: The shop's backup job on `db` has run every night since March without an error. Put ana's first restore test, and its repair, in the order lesson 12 tells it.
hint: Information Security Fundamentals, lesson 12.
items: `./backup.sh 2026-10-04` runs and prints nothing
`tar -tzf` lists `data/` and its two files
the archive is restored into an empty folder
`diff -r` against `/srv/shop` prints `Only in /srv/shop: invoices`
`sed` adds `invoices` to the `tar` line of `backup.sh`
a fresh restore compared with `diff -r` prints nothing and `exit 0`
trap: A listing from `tar -tzf` feels like proof, and stopping there is the mistake: only the restore compared with the live data showed that the invoices were never in the archive.

prompt: On 20 May the private key of `files.vereda.example` was found in a public repository, and serial `3A03` went on Vereda's CRL as Key Compromise. A machine on the path now serves the genuine `files.pem` with that key. Four clients connect to `files.vereda.example`. Which one refuses it?
hint: Applied Cryptography, lesson 9; Network Security, lesson 13.

choices.text: One run with `-k`, so that at least everything it sends stays encrypted
choices.why: Encrypted to whoever answered. `-k` skips every check, so it would accept even a certificate the impostor made itself.

choices.text: One that checks the chain against Vereda's root and the dates
choices.why: The certificate is genuine and inside its dates, so both pass. Only revocation knows the key leaked.

choices.text: One that also checks the name with `-verify_hostname`
choices.why: The name in the SAN list is exactly `files.vereda.example`. A stolen key with its real certificate passes the name check.

choices.text: One that checks `-crl_check` against the current CRL
choices.why: The CRL names `3A03`, and verification fails with `certificate revoked`. A client that does not look does not know.

prompt: A pull request to the release repository adds a line for a new key to `allowed_signers`, and changes the release script. On that branch, the release tag signed with the new key verifies as a good signature. The author asks for a quick merge because the signature checks out. What should the reviewer conclude?
hint: Applied Cryptography, lesson 6; Git and Teamwork: Version Control, Review and Process, lesson 8.

choices.text: It only says the key is listed, and this branch is what lists it, so that line needs its own review
choices.why: Whoever controls the allowed signers file decides which keys count. That is why it changes by review and is read from a protected branch.

choices.text: The tag can be trusted, since a signature only verifies when the matching private key was used to make it
choices.why: True, and it says nothing about whose key that is. The file binds names to keys, and the same branch wrote the binding.

choices.text: Ed25519 signatures are deterministic, so the reviewer can sign the tag again and compare
choices.why: Signing again needs the private key, which the reviewer does not hold, and matching bytes would prove nothing about the list.

choices.text: The `git` namespace shows the key was made for releases, so the new line is safe
choices.why: The namespace stops a signature made for one purpose being reused for another. It says nothing about who owns the key.

prompt: Vereda rehearses restoring the portal on a new machine from last night's database backup. The application starts, the store's lines begin `$argon2id$v=19$m=19456,t=2,p=1$` as before, and every staff sign-in, with the right password, answers `wrong password`. What is the likeliest cause?
hint: Applied Cryptography, lesson 5; Information Security Fundamentals, lesson 12.

choices.text: The restore gave every account a new salt, so the stored hashes no longer match
choices.why: The salt is written inside each stored string, so it came back with the database it belongs to.

choices.text: Argon2id's cost depends on the hardware, so the new machine computes different hashes
choices.why: The parameters are written into each string, `m=19456,t=2,p=1`, and give the same result on any machine.

choices.text: The pepper lives in the secrets manager, apart from the stored hashes, and the new host never got it
choices.why: Without the pepper the right password is refused, exactly as the lab showed. It is backed up separately, and a restore test has to bring it too.

choices.text: The archive was damaged in transit, which `sha256sum -c` would have reported as `FAILED`
choices.why: A damaged archive would not restore into well-formed lines that all refuse in the same way. The store is intact and missing its key.

prompt: Vereda's agenda export seals one file a day, taking the nonce from a counter in a state file, and on 8 June the export server was restored from the backup of 4 June, state file included. Had `vcrypt nonce-audit` run as a scheduled check at the end of 9 June, over `agenda-06-01.gcm` to `agenda-06-09.gcm`, how many repeated nonces would it have reported?
hint: Applied Cryptography, lesson 17.

prompt: The shop keeps `SHA256SUMS` in the same folder as its archives on the off-site disk, and checks every copy with `sha256sum -c`. ana wants the check to catch somebody who replaces an archive on purpose, too. What does that need?
hint: Applied Cryptography, lesson 6; Information Security Fundamentals, lesson 12.

choices.text: Moving from SHA-256 to SHA-512, whose longer digest is far harder to forge
choices.why: A longer hash still has no key. Whoever replaces the archive recomputes the digest just as easily.

choices.text: An HMAC or a signature in place of the plain digest, made with a key the disk does not hold
choices.why: A plain hash proves the file was not damaged, not who computed it. A keyed check cannot be redone by somebody without the key.

choices.text: Running `sha256sum -c` every night instead of only when a copy arrives
choices.why: Checking more often does not help when the person who changed the archive also rewrote `SHA256SUMS`.

choices.text: A second copy of `SHA256SUMS` in the same folder, to compare with the first
choices.why: Anybody who can write one file there can write two. Both copies end up agreeing with the replaced archive.

prompt: A review of the deployment repository finds `portal-secret.yaml`, committed months ago, with `password: Vi1kYi1zM2NyZXQtMjAyNg==` under `data:`. The developer says it is fine, because it is a Kubernetes Secret. What should the review say?
hint: Applied Cryptography, lesson 11; Git and Teamwork: Version Control, Review and Process, lesson 10.

choices.text: It is the database password in Git: `base64 -d` recovers it, so the password has to change
choices.why: Base64 is an encoding with no key, and a value in a commit stays in every clone. Only a new password makes those copies worthless.

choices.text: It is safe for as long as the cluster encrypts its datastore at rest, with a key provider behind it
choices.why: That protects the copy inside the cluster. The copy in the repository is read by anybody who can clone it.

choices.text: A new commit deleting the file is enough, since the value was only encoded
choices.why: Deleting a file does not change the commit that added it, so the value is still in the history.

choices.text: Only somebody allowed to read the Secret through `kubectl` can decode the value
choices.why: Anybody who can read the repository has the same string, and decoding it needs no access to anything.

prompt: Vereda's monitoring computes the days left on every certificate it runs, the way lesson 9 computed 154 for `portal.pem`, so that a renewal that failed silently is noticed in time. How many days before the end does lesson 9 say such a check commonly alerts? ___
hint: Applied Cryptography, lesson 9.

prompt: Three weeks after a payment key was pushed in `.env`, the team has rewritten the history with `git filter-repo`, every developer has cloned again, and `git log -S` on the new history finds nothing. The ticket asks to be closed. What is still missing?
hint: Git and Teamwork: Version Control, Review and Process, lesson 10; Applied Cryptography, lesson 17.

choices.text: A `git revert` of the commit that added the key, so the history records its removal
choices.why: After the rewrite there is no such commit to revert, and a revert never removes anything from a history.

choices.text: Revoking the key at the provider and issuing a new one, because older copies still hold it
choices.why: CI runners, a contractor's clone and the git server's backups were made before the rewrite. Only a new key makes all of them worthless.

choices.text: Nothing: once every clone was replaced, no copy with the key is left anywhere
choices.why: Replacing the clones the team controls reaches none of the copies made elsewhere during those three weeks.

choices.text: A line for `.env` in `.gitignore`, so that Git stops keeping its old versions
choices.why: `.gitignore` only keeps untracked files out of future commits. It never touches what a history already holds.

prompt: To size the incident, an analyst has to establish since when, and until when, the webhook key was in the portal's repository. Today's `settings.py` reads it from the environment. Which of these commands answer the question? Choose all that apply.
hint: Git and Teamwork: Version Control, Review and Process, lesson 3; Applied Cryptography, lesson 17.

choices.text: `git -C portal log --oneline -S "$(cat keys/webhook.hex)"`
choices.why: It lists every commit that added or removed that string: the one that brought the key in and the one that took it out.

choices.text: `git -C portal blame settings.py`
choices.why: Blame only sees lines that exist now, and the line with the key is gone from today's file.

choices.text: `git -C portal log -p | grep -nE '[0-9a-f]{64}'`
choices.why: It searches every diff in the history, and finds the key in the diff that added it and the one that removed it.

choices.text: `grep -n WEBHOOK portal/settings.py`
choices.why: It reads the file as it is today, which only shows the line reading the environment.

choices.text: `git -C portal show HEAD:settings.py`
choices.why: `HEAD` is the latest commit, the clean one. It says nothing about when the key was there.

prompt: In the portal's repository, `git log -1` on a commit that changed the payment code prints `Author: Bruno Reis <bruno.reis@vereda.example>`. Bruno says he never made it. What does that `Author` line prove?
hint: Git and Teamwork: Version Control, Review and Process, lesson 3; Applied Cryptography, lesson 6.

choices.text: That Bruno really made it, because the commit id is a hash that Git computes over everything in it, author included
choices.why: The hash makes a later edit to the author show. It says nothing about who typed the name in the first place.

choices.text: That it came from Bruno's own machine, because Git reads the author's name from his operating system account
choices.why: Git takes it from configuration or from variables such as `GIT_AUTHOR_NAME`, which is how one script made the whole week as Ana and Bruno.

choices.text: That Bruno approved it, because the platform records every merge with a name
choices.why: A review verdict is recorded beside a pull request on the hosting service. The author field is written by whoever ran `git commit`.

choices.text: Only what the committer chose to write; a signature checked against `allowed_signers` would tie it to a key
choices.why: Anybody can set the author. A signature can only be made with the private key, and the allowed signers file says whose key that is.

prompt: Ana committed `.env` with a live key and has not pushed. She runs `git reset --hard HEAD~1`, and `git log` no longer shows that commit. Which command still lists its id on her machine, for weeks? `git ___`
hint: Git and Teamwork: Version Control, Review and Process, lesson 4.

prompt: An SMS provider's key in `app.py` was committed and pushed to the shared `main` yesterday. A developer runs `git revert` on that commit and pushes the result. What has that achieved?
hint: Git and Teamwork: Version Control, Review and Process, lesson 4; Secure Coding, lesson 16.

choices.text: The commit with the key is gone from `main`, so the clones made from now on never receive it
choices.why: A revert removes nothing. It adds a commit on top, and the old one stays in the history every clone receives.

choices.text: Everybody's copy loses the key the next time they pull from the shared repository
choices.why: A pull brings the new commit. The old commit, key and all, stays in every copy.

choices.text: A new commit removes the key from the files, and the old commit still holds it
choices.why: That is what revert is for, and why the key is still exposed. Only rotation at the provider makes the copy in the history open nothing.

choices.text: The key is revoked, since the commit that carried it into `main` has been undone
choices.why: Git cannot revoke anything. The provider still accepts the key until somebody issues a new one and revokes the old.

prompt: `.env` was committed long ago and later added to `.gitignore`, yet every edit to it still shows up. Put the steps that stop Git tracking it, and keep the file on the disk, in order.
hint: Git and Teamwork: Version Control, Review and Process, lesson 10.
items: `git status --short` lists ` M .env` despite the ignore rule
`git rm --cached .env`
`git status --short` lists `D  .env`
`git commit` records the removal
`git status --short` prints nothing, and `.env` is still on the disk
trap: The ignore rule was never the missing step: `.gitignore` only applies to files Git is not already tracking, so nothing changes until `git rm --cached` takes the file out of the staging area and a commit records it.

prompt: After the fix in the hardening course, `/opt/portal/backup.sh` is `-rwxr-xr-x root root`, and root's cron still runs it at 02:30. A later check finds the folder it sits in, `/opt/portal`, is `drwxrwxrwx`. Can the `portal` account still decide what root runs tonight?
hint: Operating Systems: Windows, Linux and macOS, lesson 9; Endpoint Defence and Hardening, lesson 6.

choices.text: No: the file belongs to root and is `755`, which keeps the portal account out
choices.why: That protects the contents of the file, not its name. Removing or renaming a name is a change to the folder.

choices.text: Yes: by deleting the name and putting a file of its own there
choices.why: On a folder, `w` means create, rename and delete names inside. bruno deleted a read-only file the same way in the operating systems lesson, and the hardening rule covers the directories such a script lives in.

choices.text: Yes, by writing into the script, since `755` gives the others `x`
choices.why: `x` lets others run the file, not change it; `755` gives them no `w` on it. The way in is the folder, not the file.

choices.text: No: a folder writable by everybody carries the sticky bit, as `/tmp` does
choices.why: The sticky bit is the `t` at the end, and somebody has to set it. `drwxrwxrwx` ends in `x`, so here anybody may delete anybody's file.

prompt: Something in `/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/` changed overnight on a shared Ubuntu server. You read `journalctl _COMM=sudo` for that night, and its only entry for bruno is the command `sudo -i`, at 01:12. What does that entry establish?
hint: Operating Systems: Windows, Linux and macOS, lesson 10; SOC, Monitoring and Incident Response, lesson 2.

choices.text: That bruno edited the file, since a root shell records each command under his name
choices.why: A root shell is one command in the sudo record. What is typed inside it does not appear there, under his name or any other.

choices.text: Nothing about bruno: sudo logs refused passwords, and his was accepted
choices.why: sudo records every use, with who asked, from where, as whom and exactly what. That is what makes the line worth reading.

choices.text: That bruno opened a root shell at 01:12, and what he typed in it is not there
choices.why: The sudo record shows one command, the shell, and nothing typed inside it. Who changed the file has to come from other evidence, which is why single commands are preferred.

choices.text: That somebody logged in as root directly, which is why the record names nobody else
choices.why: Ubuntu locks root, and the entry does name a person: bruno, who borrowed the power through sudo.

prompt: The hardening ticket for `web` says avahi must be off. A colleague ran `sudo systemctl stop avahi-daemon`; now `systemctl is-active` says `inactive` and `systemctl is-enabled` says `enabled`. Which statements are right? Choose all that apply.
hint: Operating Systems: Windows, Linux and macOS, lesson 14; Endpoint Defence and Hardening, lesson 1.

choices.text: At the next boot the service starts again, because `stop` changed only what runs now
choices.why: A service has two switches. `stop` turns off the one for now and leaves the one for boot at `enabled`.

choices.text: `disable --now` would have turned off both switches in one command
choices.why: `disable` stops it starting at boot, and `--now` stops it as well, which is what a service meant to stay off needs.

choices.text: Even disabled, `avahi-daemon.socket` starts the service again on the first connection
choices.why: That is socket activation: systemd listens on the port for the service. The hardening lesson disabled the socket and the service together.

choices.text: `is-enabled` will read `disabled` once the colleague who ran `stop` logs out
choices.why: Nothing about a login changes a unit's boot switch. It stays `enabled` until somebody runs `disable`.

choices.text: `mask` would remove the package and its configuration from the machine
choices.why: That is `apt-get purge`. `mask` links the unit to `/dev/null` so nothing can start it, and leaves it installed.

choices.text: Stopping it closed its port for good, so the boot setting no longer matters
choices.why: A stopped service is closed only until the next boot, or until its socket hands the port back to it.

prompt: On a domain PC, a technician runs `reg add` on a value under `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies` to stop the screen locking. The next day the old value is back, and nobody touched the machine. What happened?
hint: Operating Systems: Windows, Linux and macOS, lesson 15; Endpoint Defence and Hardening, lesson 3.

choices.text: Group Policy writes under that key, and its next refresh wrote the policy's value back
choices.why: Policies land under `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies`, and a domain member reapplies them in the background, with security settings every 16 hours even when nothing changed. A local edit there lasts until the next refresh.

choices.text: `HKCU` holds each person's settings, and at sign-in it overrode the machine's value
choices.why: `HKCU` is one person's own tree. It does not rewrite a value in `HKLM`, and the value that came back was the machine's.

choices.text: System Restore had saved the registry, and the restart put the old copy back
choices.why: A restore point is used when somebody chooses it, from the recovery tools. An ordinary restart does not roll the registry back.

choices.text: `reg add` writes an export file, and `reg import` applies it
choices.why: It is the other way round: `reg add` changes the value at once, and `reg export` and `reg import` are the backup and the way back.

prompt: You inherit a server somebody else configured. To print only the lines of `/etc/systemd/journald.conf` that set something, hiding comments and empty lines, you run `grep ___ '^(#|$)' /etc/systemd/journald.conf`.
hint: Operating Systems: Windows, Linux and macOS, lesson 15.

prompt: Reviewing a Windows PC that restarts itself, you read its System and Security channels and find four event ids. Match each to what it says.
hint: Operating Systems: Windows, Linux and macOS, lesson 17; SOC, Monitoring and Incident Response, lesson 2.

pairs.left: 41, from Kernel-Power
pairs.right: the PC restarted without shutting down cleanly

pairs.left: 7000, from the Service Control Manager
pairs.right: a service failed to start

pairs.left: 7045, in the System channel
pairs.right: a service was installed
