hint: AI Security: Defending LLM Applications, lesson 22; SOC, Monitoring and Incident Response, lesson 6.

prompt: Match each signal at Tarefa to the rule lesson 22 gives it.
hint: AI Security: Defending LLM Applications, lesson 22.

pairs.left: a canary in a reply
pairs.right: fires on the first one, and pages

pairs.left: replies the schema refused
pairs.right: fires above three times the median of the previous 24 hours, from five events, as a ticket

pairs.left: tool calls the gate denied
pairs.right: fires above five times the median of the previous 24 hours, from ten events, as a page

pairs.left: the hourly counts themselves
pairs.right: fires when an hour goes by with no counts at all

right_distractors: fires whenever more than 2% of the hour's calls are refused, at any hour
never reaches a person, and is shown on a dashboard only

prompt: At 02:10 the canary rule pages. The reply that carried the marker quoted a version of the prompt that holds the `log-store` key. Put what the person on call does in the order lesson 24's canary runbook and INC-7 follow.
hint: AI Security: Defending LLM Applications, lesson 24; SOC, Monitoring and Incident Response, lesson 13.
items: Run `guard trace` on the call the alert names, to see which prompt and version leaked
Run `guard blast` on the key the prompt held, to see what revoking it will stop
Revoke the key, and write the step into the incident's timeline with its time
Put a replacement in the secret store, scoped to what the key's users need
Remove the key from the prompt file, in a change somebody else approves
trap: Taking the key out of the prompt feels like the fix and comes last. Done before the revocation, it is fixing it quietly: the key in the leaked reply still works for whoever read it.

prompt: On Thursday 19 November 2026, Tarefa's encarregado learns that an incident let somebody read clients' payment records, and judges it reportable. Counting as lesson 24 does, with the national holidays it lists, by the end of which day must the ANPD and the clients be told?
hint: AI Security: Defending LLM Applications, lesson 24; SOC, Monitoring and Incident Response, lesson 21.

choices.text: Sunday 22 November, three days after the Thursday
choices.why: Resolution 15 counts working days, not calendar days. A weekend never counts.

choices.text: Tuesday 24 November, counting Friday, Monday and Tuesday
choices.why: Friday 20 November is Black Consciousness Day, a national holiday on the list, so it is not a working day.

choices.text: Monday 30 November, with the time doubled to six working days
choices.why: Double time is for a small processing agent as the ANPD defines it, and nothing says Tarefa is one.

choices.text: Wednesday 25 November, past the weekend and Friday's holiday
choices.why: Thursday is day zero; Friday 20 is a holiday and the weekend follows, so Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday are working days one to three.

prompt: Tarefa plans a feature: a freelancer uploads a PDF brief, the assistant summarises it for the client, and the client gets a message when the summary is ready. The draft design gives one model the PDF's text and the `send_message` tool. Which change follows lesson 14?
hint: AI Security: Defending LLM Applications, lesson 14; Prompt Engineering, lesson 7.

choices.text: Wrap the PDF's text in a marker made fresh for each call, with a sentence saying it is material
choices.why: Markers help the code know where the client's text starts and ends. The model still reads a request inside them as a request, so they are not a boundary.

choices.text: Split it: whatever reads the brief gets no tools, and plain code does the notifying afterwards
choices.why: The more an LLM reads, the less it should be able to do. Whatever reads an attachment holds no tools, and the action is taken by code that never reads the text.

choices.text: Enforce a JSON schema on the summary, so that a request inside the PDF has nowhere to appear
choices.why: A schema bounds closed values such as a category. A summary is free text, and a request in the brief can still shape what it says.

choices.text: Keep the tool, and tell the model in the system message never to act on what a brief asks
choices.why: An instruction about instructions is one more instruction, read in the same stream as the brief. Nothing guarantees which of the two wins.

prompt: On `guard keys --now 2026-10-09`, the `orders-db` key breaks only the SCOPE rule. It was last rotated on 2026-08-20, and the inventory's limit is 90 days. If nobody rotates it, how many days after 9 October is the first `--now` date on which `guard keys` would also print AGE for it?
hint: AI Security: Defending LLM Applications, lesson 17.

prompt: On Monday an analyst reads the café agent's log. A run of the manager's task "Summarise this week's reviews" ended `stopped: 5 steps and no answer`, with two `send_email` calls to `guest@example.com`, both answered `held:`. The address appears nowhere in the manager's request. Which reading fits?
hint: Prompt Engineering, lesson 7; AI Security: Defending LLM Applications, lesson 22.

choices.text: A fetched review carried an instruction, the hold stopped it, and `reviews` is where to look
choices.why: Text the model read while doing its job asked for an e-mail, which is indirect injection. Logging every call exists so that a strange one is found and traced to its source.

choices.text: The manager's own request asked for the e-mail, which makes this direct injection by the person typing
choices.why: The task names no address. Direct injection comes from the person at the keyboard, and this request is only "Summarise this week's reviews".

choices.text: The e-mails went out, because `held:` is how `agent` reports a call that it has carried out
choices.why: `held:` means nothing is sent until a person confirms it. A call that ran prints its result instead.

choices.text: Nothing to follow up: a held call did no harm, so the entry can be closed without looking further
choices.why: An agent proposing calls outside its task is a signal worth a look, the same reading as a jump in calls the gate denied. The next run may meet a tool that is allowed.

prompt: `agent` allows `calculator`, `reviews`, `search` and `today` unless `--allow` says otherwise, and `send_email` is never on that default list. Which idea is that default?
hint: Prompt Engineering, lesson 6; Information Security Fundamentals, lesson 6.

choices.text: Cost control: an e-mail is the dearest tool in tokens, so it is left off
choices.why: Tokens are spent on text, whichever tool is named. What sets `send_email` apart is that it changes something outside the conversation.

choices.text: Model ability: a small model cannot write a valid `send_email` line
choices.why: In lesson 7's live run the model wrote that line twice. The default does not depend on what the model can write.

choices.text: Default deny: a tool that acts is given only when somebody asks
choices.why: Every task gets only the access it needs. The four on the default list only read, and the one that changes the world has to be asked for.

choices.text: Reliability: `send_email` often fails, so it waits until it is fixed
choices.why: It is not broken. `agent` holds it by design, and with `--allow` it is offered and then held for a person.

prompt: The café's triage replies sometimes add a `mood` field, and each one costs a retry. A colleague proposes deleting `"additionalProperties": false` from `schema.json` so that those replies pass. What do the two lessons say?
hint: Prompt Engineering, lesson 19; Secure Coding, lesson 2.

choices.text: Delete it: the program only reads the fields it knows, so an extra one cannot harm anything
choices.why: Without that line a program carries an unexpected field along without anybody deciding that it should.

choices.text: Replace it with a list of refused field names, starting with `mood` and adding more as they appear
choices.why: That is a denylist, and it has to know every bad value in advance. The next unwanted field is one nobody has listed yet.

choices.text: Delete it and switch on constrained decoding, which makes every reply that passes correct
choices.why: Decoding follows whatever schema it is given, so without the line it allows extra fields too, and a valid reply can still be wrong.

choices.text: Keep it: the schema is an allowlist, which names the valid fields and refuses all the rest
choices.why: A check that describes what is good refuses what nobody thought of. The retry is the price of a reply that did not match, paid in the open.

prompt: The café adds a canary marker to its system prompt and a filter that blocks any reply containing it. A colleague says the staff discount code can now go in the system prompt too, because a leak would be caught. What is wrong with that?
hint: Prompt Engineering, lesson 22; AI Security: Defending LLM Applications, lesson 5.

choices.text: Nothing, provided the prompt also says never to reveal the code, since the system message takes precedence
choices.why: The precedence of a system message is trained, not enforced. A user message or a document can still win.

choices.text: A canary shows only the prompt repeated word for word, and the code alone or reworded slips past
choices.why: A reply can carry the code without the marker, and the canary sees nothing. If the model must not tell it, the model must not be given it.

choices.text: Nothing, provided the code sits on the marker's own line, so any reply quoting it carries both
choices.why: A reply can quote part of a line, or give the code in words of its own. The marker travels only with a verbatim copy.

choices.text: Only its cost: the 149-token prompt grows by a few tokens, paid again on every single request
choices.why: The cost is real and small. The problem is that a system prompt can be revealed, so a secret in it is a secret on its way out.

prompt: The café's assistant summarises supplier invoices. One invoice holds a line addressed to the assistant, asking it to change the bank details on file. Lesson 7 calls an instruction that arrives this way, inside text the model reads while doing its job, ___ prompt injection.
hint: Prompt Engineering, lesson 7.

prompt: The café connects its assistant's `search` tool to the whole shared drive, so that it can answer customers from the handbook. The drive also holds the payroll, and the system prompt says payroll is never to be quoted. Which changes keep payroll lines out of replies to customers, however a question is worded? Choose all that apply.
hint: Prompt Engineering, lesson 7; AI Security: Defending LLM Applications, lesson 15.

choices.text: Point the search at the handbook alone, so payroll text never reaches the context
choices.why: A search tool for this task should read the handbook and not the payroll. What is never in the context cannot come out in a reply.

choices.text: Repeat the payroll rule at the end of the system prompt as well as at the start
choices.why: Repeating a rule in the prompt is still a request the model weighs against everything else in its input.

choices.text: Filter what is searched by what the person asking is allowed to read, before ranking
choices.why: Access control decides which documents reach the prompt. A customer may not read payroll, so payroll is never a candidate.

choices.text: Wrap each search result in `<untrusted>` and `</untrusted>` before it reaches the model
choices.why: The marking tells the model which text is data. The payroll line is still in the context, and the model can still repeat it.

choices.text: Run the assistant at temperature 0, so it never improvises a salary figure
choices.why: Temperature changes how the next word is drawn. A salary that is in the context can be copied at any temperature.

prompt: An app puts the rule `Never ask for card numbers` in the first user message of each chat instead of the system message. When a long chat outgrows the window, the program trims it before sending, and the usual rule drops the ___ turns first, so that rule is lost while the system message stays.
hint: Prompt Engineering, lesson 4.

prompt: A demo of the shop's support agent ran its tools with ana's own AWS credentials, which have gathered permissions over two years of her work. The agent is about to go to production. What do the two lessons say?
hint: AI in Development, lesson 7; Cloud Security, lesson 6.

choices.text: Give the agent its own credentials, scoped to its tools, since hers hold all she was granted
choices.why: Granted access only grows, and an agent running as ana can do all of it. Least access for an agent means its own identity, narrowed to its tools.

choices.text: Keep hers, and require a second factor at sign-in, which makes the agent's calls safe enough
choices.why: A second factor protects a person signing in. The agent's calls would still carry every permission she holds, and machines are not people.

choices.text: Keep hers, because a person's credentials leave an audit trail that names somebody responsible
choices.why: The trail would name the wrong somebody: every call the agent makes would read as ana's own, with her whole reach behind it.

choices.text: Keep hers, and rely on the approval prompt to stop anything the agent should not do with them
choices.why: Approval covers the calls the host asks about. Limits belong below the model, and the credentials are what bound everything else.

prompt: A model suggests the package `money` for the cart's prices. `check_package.py` finds it on PyPI, first release 2013-11-16 and last 2016-04-17, and `pip-audit` reports no advisory against it. Is that enough to add it?
hint: AI in Development, lesson 11; Secure Coding, lesson 17.

choices.text: Yes: it exists, so it is not an invented name, and the audit came back clean
choices.why: Existing settles only the first question. A clean audit says no published advisory matches today, and nothing about who will fix the next one.

choices.text: Yes, as long as it is pinned, since a pin keeps its code from ever changing
choices.why: A pin stops the code changing under you. It does not make anybody maintain it, and an idle package has no fixed version to move to.

choices.text: No: an audit sees only published advisories, and an idle package gets no fixes
choices.why: An advisory against an unmaintained library has no fixed version to move to. The shop already keeps money as integer cents, so the dependency buys nothing.

choices.text: No: `money` is a name the model made up, as `cartmoney` was
choices.why: The check found `money` on PyPI with releases and a summary. `cartmoney` was the name that was not there.

prompt: A review bot reads a pull request that adds the route `GET /invoices/<id>`. It posts three findings about naming and type hints, and says nothing about who may call the route. What should the person reviewing the change do?
hint: AI in Development, lesson 4; Secure Coding, lesson 18.

choices.text: Approve it: the bot read every line, so a missing check would have been one of its findings
choices.why: A missing check is invisible in the code that is there. A reviewer that misses something says nothing, and the silence reads like approval.

choices.text: Settle the three findings first, since a review spends its time in the order the findings arrive
choices.why: A security review spends its budget in order of what a mistake would cost, and naming comes last.

choices.text: Ask the bot again for security problems only, and merge the change if it then finds none
choices.why: A second answer is another claim. The bot informs the person who decides and never holds the decision to merge.

choices.text: Ask who is allowed to call it and whether the invoice must be the caller's, and pin that with a test
choices.why: "Who may do this?" comes first because the reviewer has to ask about a line that is absent. A test turns the answer into something that fails if it changes.

prompt: The shop's agent asked for `issue_refund` with `"cents": "0"` on an order of 79.80, the operator answered `y`, and a refund of zero was paid and logged. Which change refuses a call like that whoever approves it?
hint: AI in Development, lesson 7; AI Security: Defending LLM Applications, lesson 10.

choices.text: Show the operator a short summary, such as "a refund for order 1042", instead of the raw arguments
choices.why: That hides the zero that was in plain sight. A person approving "a refund" is not approving "a refund of 0 cents on order 1042".

choices.text: Make `issue_refund` refuse any amount below one cent or above what the order cost
choices.why: The tool is the one place every call passes through. A limit a person could override by clicking would be a suggestion; Tarefa's gate refuses a refund above what was paid before anybody is asked.

choices.text: Ask a second operator to approve every refund as well as the first one
choices.why: Another person is another check, and both can answer `y` to the same screen. Nothing in the flow says what amount is allowed.

choices.text: Tell the model in its system prompt that a refund must always be above zero
choices.why: A line in the prompt is a request the model may not follow. The rule has to be an `if` in code that runs whoever asked.

prompt: The sign-in route fails on the staging server, and the error was logged with its traceback. Before asking an assistant about it, which of these belong in the request? Choose all that apply.
hint: AI in Development, lesson 5; Secure Coding, lesson 15.

choices.text: The traceback as the program wrote it, with the password in the connection string taken out
choices.why: The traceback is the best evidence there is, unedited, except for the one thing that comes out first: a secret.

choices.text: The log lines around the error, session token and all, so the model sees the whole request
choices.why: A log line can carry a token, and a token pasted into a request has left your control. A log is read by more people than anybody remembers.

choices.text: The exact command or request that produced the error
choices.why: The command makes the input exact, which a description cannot do.

choices.text: The project's `.env`, so the model can see how the database is set up
choices.why: A `.env` holds the secrets the rest of the course keeps out of every file an assistant reads.

choices.text: The version of the library the route uses, as `pip list` prints it
choices.why: When the problem might be a version, the version line answers it.

choices.text: A short description in your own words in place of the traceback, to keep the request small
choices.why: A description says "it crashes". The traceback says which file, which line and which value, and it is shorter to copy than to describe.

prompt: ana asks `assist` a question with three files open. Put what `assist` does with the open files in the order its code does it, before the model sees anything.
hint: AI in Development, lesson 3.
items: Skip each file whose path is listed in `.assistignore`, without opening it
Refuse, whole, each remaining file whose text matches the secret pattern
Add the files left, in the order they were opened, while the 3,000-token budget lasts
Send the gathered context to the model, with the question
trap: The secret pattern cannot come first: a file on `.assistignore` is never opened, so it has no text to match. That is also why the list catches `settings.py` when the pattern does not.

prompt: A product page renders the model's rewrite of each customer review with `{{ review|safe }}`, because "the model wrote it, so it is our own HTML". What do the two lessons say about that filter here?
hint: AI in Development, lesson 11; Secure Coding, lesson 4.

choices.text: It is fine, because the model was asked for HTML and so its reply is HTML the application generated
choices.why: The model copies what it read, and what it read was written by a customer. Lesson 11's rewrite kept the review's `<script>` tag.

choices.text: It is fine if the prompt tells the model to remove every script tag before it answers
choices.why: That is a request the model may not follow, and a script tag is only one of the ways markup becomes code.

choices.text: It is the mistake: `safe` is for HTML the application made, not for text a person typed
choices.why: The model's reply is untrusted input that looks like your program's output. Let the template escape it, as it would any other user content.

choices.text: It is the mistake, and the fix is to escape the review text once before it is sent to the model
choices.why: Escaping belongs at the point where text becomes HTML. Escaping the input changes what the model reads and leaves its reply unescaped.

prompt: A candidate's home-lab repository is public. Its first commit included `.env`, holding a token for the lab's SIEM, and a later commit added `.env` to `.gitignore`. After an edit, `git status --short` still lists the file as modified. Which step comes first?
hint: The Portfolio Project: From Brief to Deploy, lesson 14; Git and Teamwork: Version Control, Review and Process, lesson 10.

choices.text: Run `git rm --cached .env` and commit, which takes the token out of the history
choices.why: That stops tracking the file from the next commit on; the commit that added it still holds the token, in every clone.

choices.text: Revoke the token at the SIEM that issued it, before touching git at all
choices.why: A secret that reached a public repository is treated as known, and revoking is the one step that makes the copy useless. The ignore rule is a second problem: `.gitignore` only applies to files git is not already tracking.

choices.text: Rewrite the history with `git filter-repo`, force-push, then deal with the token
choices.why: Cleaning the history is optional and comes last: it cannot reach the clones and caches made before it, and a tidy history with a live token is still an open door.

choices.text: Nothing yet: the ignore rule takes effect after the next edit of the file
choices.why: No edit changes it. Git keeps tracking a file that is in the history, and the token stays readable in the first commit meanwhile.

prompt: A candidate wants to move the lab server of lesson 15 to a rented server with a public address, reusing the same `srv.yaml`, the same key and the same Caddyfile. Which of these does the lesson say has to change on the way? Choose all that apply.
hint: The Portfolio Project: From Brief to Deploy, lesson 15.

choices.text: The `sudo` line with `NOPASSWD:ALL`, acceptable only where your computer alone reaches the machine
choices.why: The lesson calls sudo without a password fine on a machine only your computer reaches, and wrong on a public one.

choices.text: The key made with `-N ""`, because a key that opens anything public gets a passphrase
choices.why: Leaving the private half without a passphrase was a fair trade for one machine on a private network, and the lesson says so in those terms.

choices.text: The `tls internal` line, so that Caddy obtains its certificate from a public authority
choices.why: With a public name Caddy gets the certificate by itself, and needs ports 80 and 443 reachable to prove it controls the name.

choices.text: `ssh_pwauth: false`, so a password still lets you in if the key is ever lost
choices.why: Password logins stay off on purpose. A lost key is solved the way the lesson solves a wrong one: build the machine again.

choices.text: `PublishPort=127.0.0.1:8000:8000`, so visitors can reach the container without Caddy
choices.why: Publishing on `127.0.0.1` is what makes Caddy the only door; opening it would serve the application around HTTPS.

choices.text: `USER 1000` in the Containerfile, since a public server needs the program running as root
choices.why: The container still listens on 8000 behind Caddy. `USER 1000` is what stops a bug in the program from acting as root, on any server.

prompt: A junior analyst has looked after `srv` for months and has not rebuilt it. One morning `ssh srv` prints `WARNING: REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED!` and suggests an `ssh-keygen -R` command to forget the old key. What should happen before anybody runs it?
hint: The Portfolio Project: From Brief to Deploy, lesson 15; Network Security, lesson 11.

choices.text: Run it: the warning names the command, and that command fixes it
choices.why: The lesson runs `ssh-keygen -R` when you rebuilt srv yourself. Nobody did here, so the reason for the new key is still unknown.

choices.text: Accept the new key when ssh asks, since the address is still srv's
choices.why: An impostor would answer from the same address. Saying yes without comparing trusts whoever answered first.

choices.text: Turn host-key checking off for srv, so the same warning stops coming back
choices.why: The fix for a check that gets in the way is to distribute the right keys in advance, never to switch the check off.

choices.text: Find out why the key changed, comparing the new fingerprint with one read on srv
choices.why: This is the warning that would catch somebody impersonating your server. A fingerprint only proves something when it was obtained another way, such as `ssh-keygen -lf` run on srv itself.

prompt: Reviewing her own pull request, a candidate sees that `list.innerHTML = items.map(row).join("")` builds the loan table, and that `row` puts each borrower's name in as typed. A name is saved by one teacher and shown to every other. What is this, and what fix do the lessons use?
hint: The Portfolio Project: From Brief to Deploy, lesson 10; Secure Coding, lesson 7.

choices.text: Stored cross-site scripting; build each row of the table with `textContent`
choices.why: Text saved first and shown later to other people is the stored kind, and `textContent` sets text and parses nothing.

choices.text: Reflected cross-site scripting; escape the name in the request that echoes it
choices.why: Reflected text arrives in a request and goes back to the same person. This name was saved, and every other teacher sees it.

choices.text: DOM-based cross-site scripting; ignore whatever follows the `#` in the address
choices.why: The DOM-based kind reads the address after `#`. These names come from the server's list, not from the address.

choices.text: A slip the `grep` over added lines flags; delete the line, commit again
choices.why: The lesson says no grep finds it; the checklist's question about user input drawn as HTML does. The line also predates this change.

prompt: An analyst wants loanbook's `app.log`, with lines such as `POST /api/items/1/loan 409`, joined with the firewall's records in the SIEM. Which change lets those lines be joined and still keeps the portfolio lesson's rule for what this log says?
hint: The Portfolio Project: From Brief to Deploy, lesson 11; SOC, Monitoring and Incident Response, lesson 1.

choices.text: Add each request's body, so the analyst can see who borrowed what
choices.why: The body holds people's names, and a log is kept longer and read by more people than the database is.

choices.text: Leave it: method, path and status already answer what a log should
choices.why: The line says what and with what outcome, but not when or from where, and a join needs fields the two records share.

choices.text: Bring back the time, with its zone, and the client's address; keep the body out
choices.why: loanbook's override dropped exactly the date and the client's address, which are the when and the from-where a log needs to be joined. The body stays out because it holds names.

choices.text: Write a traceback for each `4xx` answer, so that every refusal is on the record too
choices.why: A traceback is for the unexpected. A `409` is a rule saying no, and the status at the end of the line already records it.

prompt: A candidate's security portfolio is a written assessment of a deliberately vulnerable application in a home lab. One finding reads only: *The login form is vulnerable to SQL injection. Severity: high.* What else do the two lessons ask this finding to carry?
hint: The Portfolio Project: From Brief to Deploy, lesson 3; SOC, Monitoring and Incident Response, lesson 20.

choices.text: The name of the scanner that found it, which gives the finding its weight
choices.why: A tool's name lets nobody check the claim. A reader who asks wants to see what was sent and what came back.

choices.text: A single score for the whole application, so clients can compare it
choices.why: The report a client can act on is built finding by finding; one number for the application tells nobody what to change.

choices.text: The word *likely*, so the claim cannot be held against the author
choices.why: Confirmed and likely describe what the evidence shows. A reproduced request is a confirmed fact, and hedging it is not honesty.

choices.text: The evidence a reader could check, and what to do about the flaw
choices.why: The portfolio lesson asks for findings with severity, evidence and what to do about each, and the report lesson says every claim must be checkable from its source.

prompt: loanbook's unit file sets `HealthInterval=30s`, and lesson 15 warns that a service calling a model should not have a health check that spends money on every run. If each check made one paid call, how many calls would that come to in one day?
hint: The Portfolio Project: From Brief to Deploy, lesson 15.

prompt: A candidate builds the lab server of lesson 15 on a laptop that has no SSH key yet. Put the steps in the order the lesson takes them.
hint: The Portfolio Project: From Brief to Deploy, lesson 15.
items: Make a key pair with `ssh-keygen -t ed25519`
Paste the public half into `srv.yaml`, under `ssh_authorized_keys`
Create the machine with `multipass launch` and `--cloud-init srv.yaml`
Add a `Host srv` entry to `~/.ssh/config` with the address `multipass info` printed
Compare the fingerprint and answer the first-connection question
Wait with `cloud-init status --wait` before asking for the tools
trap: The key comes before the machine: cloud-init reads `srv.yaml` only on the first boot, so a key pasted in after `launch` changes nothing on a machine that already exists.

prompt: A candidate drafts the CV line for a home-lab SOC project and tries four fragments. Match each fragment to what lesson 4 says about it.
hint: From Study to Hired: CV, Interviews and the First 90 Days, lesson 4; SOC, Monitoring and Incident Response, lesson 15.

pairs.left: *Detected 100% of attacks in my home lab*
pairs.right: a number that cannot say how it was measured, or against what

pairs.left: *Helped set up a SIEM with a study group*
pairs.right: a verb that hides which part was yours

pairs.left: *Developed a lab using Python, sqlite and Sigma*
pairs.right: the stack, which fits ten thousand CVs

pairs.left: *a Sigma rule that fires on a test event and shows in the SIEM*
pairs.right: the shown-by part: evidence anybody can check

right_distractors: the which part: what is true now that was not
a baseline, which turns a number into a finding

prompt: In your third week as a SOC analyst, you closed yesterday's alert from `203.0.113.66` as a false positive, with the reason *known user*. This morning the account's own history shows it had never logged in from that address before. What do the two lessons say to do first?
hint: From Study to Hired: CV, Interviews and the First 90 Days, lesson 20; SOC, Monitoring and Incident Response, lesson 7.

choices.text: Tell the shift lead now that you closed it, and why you think it is real
choices.why: Say it early to the person who needs to know. A closed true alert is the costliest mistake in a SOC because nothing downstream looks at it again, so until you speak nobody will.

choices.text: Reopen it and look into it alone, so that the lead hears a finished answer
choices.why: An hour of silence while you try to fix it alone turns a small mistake into an incident, and whoever used the account keeps that hour.

choices.text: Leave it closed and wait: if it is real, the rule will fire again
choices.why: A rule fires on events, and nothing says the next ones will match. The closed alert is the one record nobody downstream will reopen.

choices.text: Rewrite the closure note in full, so that the next analyst sees what you saw
choices.why: A better note on a closed alert changes nobody's priority. It needs a person working it now, not a fuller record.

prompt: Asked *tell me about a time you failed*, a candidate answers with the postmortem of a home-lab incident, in its own words: *the server accepted passwords from the internet, and alerts reached nobody at night.* Those sentences were right in the postmortem. Why do they fall short here?
hint: From Study to Hired: CV, Interviews and the First 90 Days, lesson 15; SOC, Monitoring and Incident Response, lesson 15.

choices.text: They should name whoever chose the weak password, so the result is honest
choices.why: Pointing at somebody else is the failure answer that blames. The question is about your own part.

choices.text: They are too short: a two-minute answer needs the intervals from `milestones.sql` added as well
choices.why: Intervals are situation, and the situation gets about a tenth of the time. The action is what the interviewer is asking about.

choices.text: A postmortem looks for conditions; the interview asks what *you* did and what changed after
choices.why: Blameless wording suits a review that changes systems. A failure answer is a STAR story whose action says *I* and whose last sentence is what changed.

choices.text: They do not: conditions with no culprit are what that question listens for
choices.why: The failure answer that fails is the one with no failure in it, and conditions with nobody acting have none.

prompt: A candidate times a STAR answer about a home-lab incident at two minutes. If the four parts take the shares lesson 15 gives them, about how many seconds go to the Action?
hint: From Study to Hired: CV, Interviews and the First 90 Days, lesson 15.

prompt: In a SOC, the first thing you ship is often the first alert you close on your own. Lesson 20 says a ticket closed well states what was wrong, what you did, and how you ___ it. Which word fills the blank?
hint: From Study to Hired: CV, Interviews and the First 90 Days, lesson 20.

prompt: In an interview for a SOC role you are asked: *how would you have our SOAR contain a compromised account on its own, end to end?* You have never run a SOAR outside a lab. Which answer follows lesson 14?
hint: From Study to Hired: CV, Interviews and the First 90 Days, lesson 14; SOC, Monitoring and Incident Response, lesson 5.

choices.text: Lay out a design in which the playbook disables the account and wipes the laptop by itself
choices.why: A confident answer that is wrong costs the most, and disabling an account and wiping a laptop are the steps the SOAR lesson keeps from a machine.

choices.text: Say you have not run one, that disabling an account needs a person's call, and how you would try it
choices.why: Lesson 14's three steps: say it plainly, say what you know nearby, and say how you would find out. The nearby fact is the SOAR lesson's: disabling an account takes judgement about who it is.

choices.text: Explain that SOAR exists to respond faster than people, so all of it gets automated
choices.why: That is the common belief the SOAR lesson corrects: most of the value is the enrichment before the decision, which stays a person's.

choices.text: Say you do not know SOAR, and wait for the next question
choices.why: That is the first of three steps and stops there. What you know nearby, and how you would find out, is what the interviewer is watching for.
